decisions.prompt: Your cold boot took far longer than your neighbour's, and the screen mentioned Windows updates. What do you put in your table?

options.consequence: The result is honest, and the note names a real source of error: background updates slow some boots.

options.text: Your neighbour's time, since yours looks wrong
options.consequence: That is not your measurement, so the table no longer describes your computer.

options.text: Nothing yet: switch off at the UPS and boot again
options.consequence: Cutting the power during an update can corrupt files, and the machine may then fail to start.

decisions.prompt: You must now warm boot the computer. Which action do you take?

options.text: Start > Power > Restart
options.consequence: Windows closes in an orderly way and starts again: that is a warm boot.

options.text: Hold the power button until the screen goes dark
options.consequence: That forces a working computer off. Files can be damaged, and it is not a warm boot.

options.text: Switch off the UPS, then switch it back on
options.consequence: That removes the power, so it would be a cold start, and Windows was still running.

decisions.prompt: The bell has gone and your notes are still open in a program. What do you do first?

options.consequence: Your work is safe and Windows closes cleanly.

options.text: Turn the monitor off and leave the computer running
options.consequence: The screen is dark but the computer has not shut down, and your file is still unsaved.

decisions.prompt: You have chosen Shut down. The screen says "Shutting down" and the power light is still on. What now?

options.consequence: Windows finishes closing its files before any power is removed.

options.text: Switch off the UPS now to save time before the next class
options.consequence: The power goes while Windows is still writing to the disk, which can corrupt files.

options.text: Pull the power cable from the back of the system unit
options.consequence: That cuts the power during shut-down and handles a live connection for no reason.

options.text: The screen says "Shutting down"

options.text: The Start menu opens by itself
options.why: The POST is a hardware check before any Windows feature exists.

options.text: Monitor

options.text: System unit
options.why: That is hardware, not a screen feature.

faults.scenario: Ngozi's table of boot times looks odd, and the computer complained about files the next day. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She held the power button down to end the session, although Windows was working normally.

lines.text: She wrote "keyboard" and "mouse" in her list of desktop features.
lines.why: Those are hardware. Desktop features include icons, the Start button and the taskbar.

lines.text: She labelled the restart from the Start menu as a cold boot.
lines.why: A restart of a running computer is a warm boot. A cold boot starts from power off.

lines.text: She switched on the UPS, then the monitor, then the system unit.
lines.why: That is the correct order.

lines.text: She stopped the timer when the busy circle had gone from the pointer.

options.consequence: The extra time is only a guess, so the timing is no longer exact.

options.consequence: Backspace deletes to the left of the cursor, which is the wrong letter.

options.consequence: Esc does not remove text in Notepad, so the mistake stays.

options.consequence: Net speed is reduced by uncorrected errors, so your count is correct.

options.text: Every time you pressed Backspace while typing
options.consequence: Those mistakes were corrected. They cost you time but are not counted again.

options.text: None, as long as the passage can still be read
options.consequence: Net speed needs the uncorrected errors, so your result would be too high.

options.why: Cursor keys are the arrows.

options.text: Alphabetic keys

A student typed {c} characters in {m} minutes and left {e} uncorrected errors. A standard word is 5 characters. What is the net speed in wpm?

faults.scenario: Emeka got 300 wpm for a typing test, which cannot be true. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He divided his characters by the minutes and called that his speed.
lines.why: Characters must first be divided by 5 to give words. He forgot that step.

lines.text: He kept typing for a while after the stopwatch reached the limit.
lines.why: The extra typing inflates the count. Stop exactly at the time limit.

lines.text: He described the numeric keypad as the function keys.
lines.why: Function keys are F1 to F12. The keypad holds numeric keys.

lines.text: He used the word processor's count to find his number of characters.
lines.why: That is the right way to get an exact figure.

lines.text: He returned his fingers to the home keys after each stroke.
lines.why: That is correct typing technique.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for a fair and comfortable typing test.
written.explainPrompt: Why is the number of characters divided by 5 before the typing speed is worked out?
written.explainGuide: A standard word is taken as 5 characters, including spaces. Dividing by 5 turns characters into standard words, so that speeds can be compared fairly in words per minute however long the real words are.

numerics.working: One way: floor(210/90) x floor(297/55) = 2 x 5 = 10. Turned round: floor(210/55) x floor(297/90) = 3 x 3 = 9. Choose {answer}.

decisions.prompt: You are about to convert the capacities on your table. Which conversion factor do you use?

options.text: 1 024 between each unit and the next
options.consequence: Computer storage works in powers of 2, so the lesson's 1 024 is correct.

options.text: 1 000 between each unit and the next
options.consequence: Manufacturers quote that way, but this exercise uses 1 024, and your answers would be wrong.

options.text: 8 between each unit and the next
options.consequence: Eight is only the number of bits in a byte, not the step between KB, MB and GB.

decisions.prompt: You need to change 5 120 KB into MB. What do you do with the 1 024?

options.text: Divide, because the unit is getting larger
options.consequence: A larger unit gives a smaller number: 5 120 / 1 024 = 5 MB.

options.text: Multiply, because the unit is getting larger
options.consequence: The number becomes huge, which is a common mistake in this topic.

options.text: Subtract it from the figure once for each unit
options.consequence: Unit conversions need multiplying or dividing, never subtracting.

options.consequence: Six discs cannot hold all the data. Some of it is left over.

options.text: 6.88 CDs
options.consequence: You cannot use part of a disc, so the answer must be a whole number.

The RAM is several times bigger than the hard disk

options.why: They do different jobs and differ greatly in size.

observations.prompt: You copy a file to the flash drive and look again at its free space. What should have happened?

Free space rose by the size of the file
options.why: Adding a file uses up space.

options.text: Free space stayed exactly the same
options.why: The file is now stored there and takes up room.

options.text: Total capacity of the drive fell by the file size
options.why: Total size is fixed. Only the free space changes.

decisions.prompt: You have the column of remainders for 45 divided by 2. In what order do you write them?

distractors.why: No network is involved. The truth table is worked out by hand.

distractors.name: Protractor
distractors.why: No angles are measured here.

optional: Optional: online logic simulator or a breadboard with 7408 (AND), 7432 (OR) and 7404 (NOT) chips, LEDs and a 5 V supply

decisions.prompt: You must set out the input combinations for A, B and C. How do you list them?

options.text: In binary counting order, from 000 to 111
options.consequence: All 8 rows appear exactly once, and none is missed.

options.text: In whatever order you think of them
options.consequence: It is easy to repeat or miss a row, and you would lose the marks for it.

options.text: Only the rows where the output will be 1
options.consequence: A truth table needs every combination, including those that give 0.

decisions.prompt: You have written six rows and cannot think of another. What do you decide?

options.text: Add two more, as three inputs give eight rows
options.consequence: 2^3 = 8, so the table is now complete.

options.text: Stop at six, one pair of rows for each input
options.consequence: Six is a common wrong count. Some of the combinations are still missing.

options.text: Stop at three, one row for each input
options.consequence: A truth table needs every combination, not one row per input.

decisions.prompt: How do you lay out the table to find X for each row?

options.text: Give A.B and C' their own columns before X
options.consequence: The intermediate columns reduce slips and earn method marks.

options.text: Go straight to X and do the rest in your head
options.consequence: Slips go unnoticed, and the method marks for those columns are lost.

options.text: Add a column for A + B, then find X from it
options.consequence: A + B is not part of X = A.B + C', so that column leads you astray.

decisions.prompt: On the breadboard, one row of your table does not match the LED. What do you do first?

options.text: Switch off, then check the wiring for loose links
options.consequence: Loose breadboard connections are a common source of error, and it is safe to work on with the power off.

options.text: Change the table to match what the LED shows
options.consequence: A wiring fault has now been copied into your work and hidden.

options.text: Move the wires around with the supply still on
options.consequence: A slip can short the circuit. Always switch off before changing wiring.

observations.prompt: You step through all the input combinations for X = A.B + C'. What should the LED show?

options.text: On for 5 of the 8 combinations
On for 4 of the 8 combinations
options.why: Count again: X is 1 for every row with C = 0, and for 111.

options.text: On only for 111
options.why: X is also 1 whenever C = 0.

options.text: On for all 8 combinations
options.why: X is 0 for 001, 011 and 101.

observations.prompt: Which gate gives an output of 0 only when both of its inputs are 1?

options.text: NAND
AND
options.why: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1.

options.text: NOR
options.why: NOR gives 1 only when both inputs are 0.

options.text: XOR
options.why: XOR gives 1 when its inputs differ.

numerics.prompt: How many rows does the truth table of a circuit with {n} inputs have?
For X = A.B + C', find X when A = {a}, B = {b} and C = {c}.
numerics.working: A.B = {a} x {b}. C' is the opposite of {c}. OR gives 1 if either is 1, so X = {answer}.

numerics.prompt: In the full truth table of X = A.B + C', in how many rows is X equal to 1?
numerics.working: X = 1 for 000, 010, 100, 110 and 111: that is {answer} rows.

faults.scenario: Kemi's logic work lost marks in several places. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She drew the OR gate with a flat back.
lines.why: A flat back belongs to AND. The OR gate has a curved back.

lines.text: She drew the NAND gate without the small bubble at its output.
lines.why: The bubble shows the inversion on NOT, NAND and NOR.

lines.text: She gave six rows for her three-input table.
lines.why: Three inputs need 2^3 = 8 rows.

lines.text: She listed her inputs from 000 to 111 in counting order.
lines.why: That makes sure no row is missed.

lines.text: She added columns for A.B and C' before the column for X.
lines.why: Those intermediate columns earn method marks.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions when drawing logic circuits and building truth tables.
written.explainPrompt: Why does a truth table with three inputs have eight rows?
written.explainGuide: Each input can be 0 or 1, giving two choices. With three inputs the number of combinations is 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3 = 8, and a truth table must show every combination, so it needs eight rows.

correct: Walk carefully round the laboratory and do not step on cables or trunking.

wrong.text: Unplug a cable from the switch to see which computer loses its connection.
wrong.why: That disrupts other users' work. Do not unplug network devices without permission.

wrong.text: Lift the cover off the trunking to count the cables inside.
wrong.why: That can damage the installation. Count from the visible ends or ask the teacher.

wrong.text: Press the reset button on the router to find out what it does.
wrong.why: A reset can wipe its settings and take the whole network down.

wrong.text: Stand on a chair to read the label on a wall-mounted switch.
wrong.why: A chair can tip over. Ask the teacher to read it or show you a picture.

wrong.text: Switch off the modem to see whether anything changes in the laboratory.
wrong.why: That cuts off the network for everyone. Never do it without permission.

distractors.name: Crimping tool
distractors.why: No cables are made in this practical. You observe and draw.

distractors.name: Network cable tester
distractors.why: Cables are counted and drawn, not tested.

distractors.name: Flash drive
distractors.why: Nothing is copied or stored in this job.

distractors.name: Soldering iron
distractors.why: There is no electronic repair in this job.

distractors.name: Protractor
distractors.why: Topology diagrams show connections, not exact angles.

decisions.prompt: You are drawing the star. What goes at the centre of your diagram?

options.text: The switch
options.consequence: In a star layout every cable runs from a computer to the central switch.

options.text: The first computer in the row
options.consequence: Then that computer would have to carry all the links, which is not a star.

options.text: The modem
options.consequence: A modem links the network to the Internet service. It does not join the computers.

decisions.prompt: What must you show at both ends of the bus backbone?

options.text: A terminator
options.consequence: Terminators stop signals bouncing back along the cable.

options.text: A switch
options.consequence: A central switch or hub does not belong in a bus layout, which is a common mistake.

options.text: A router
options.consequence: A router joins networks. It does not finish off a backbone.

decisions.prompt: The school wants one faulty cable to stop only one computer. Which layout do you recommend?

options.text: Star, with a cable from each computer to the switch
options.consequence: A bad cable affects only its own computer, as in the laboratory.

options.text: Bus, with a single backbone for all the computers
options.consequence: A break in the backbone can stop the whole network.

options.text: Ring, with each computer joined to two neighbours
options.consequence: A break in a simple ring can stop traffic round the whole ring.

observations.prompt: You follow the cables in the laboratory. Which finding means that it is a star?

options.text: Every cable runs from a computer to the switch
All the computers tap into one long cable
options.why: That describes a bus.

options.text: Each computer is joined to two neighbours
options.why: That describes a ring.

observations.prompt: You are labelling the devices. Which description fits the router?

options.text: It connects the LAN to other networks such as the Internet
It is fitted inside each computer to join it to the cable
options.why: That is the network interface card.

options.text: It closes the end of a bus backbone
options.why: That is a terminator.

options.text: It joins the computers of one room to each other
options.why: That is the job of the switch.

numerics.prompt: A {p}-port switch connects {n} computers in a star. How many ports are free?
A ring joins {n} computers, each to two neighbours. How many links are needed?
numerics.working: A ring of {n} computers closes with one link per computer: {answer} links.

numerics.prompt: How many cables does a star network of {n} computers need?
numerics.working: One cable per computer to the switch: {answer} cables.

faults.scenario: Ike's network diagrams lost marks. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He drew a hub in the middle of his bus topology.
lines.why: A bus has a single backbone and no central device.

lines.text: He described the network of the school laboratory as a WAN.
lines.why: A network in one building is a LAN. A WAN covers a wide area.

lines.text: He left the devices in his diagrams unlabelled.
lines.why: Each device must be labelled to earn the marks.

lines.text: He gave each computer two neighbours in his ring.
lines.why: That is a correct ring.

lines.text: He ended the bus backbone with two terminators.
lines.why: That is correct for a bus.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for touring the laboratory and drawing its network.
written.explainPrompt: Why does a fault in one cable of a star network affect only one computer?
written.explainGuide: In a star, each computer has its own cable to the central switch. If one cable fails, only that computer is cut off, and the others keep working through their own cables.

correct: Tell the teacher at once if the antivirus reports a threat on a school computer.

wrong.text: Open a file that the antivirus has flagged, to see what it really is.
wrong.why: A flagged file can infect the computer when it runs. Quarantine it and tell the teacher.

wrong.text: Turn off the antivirus because it is slowing down your work.
wrong.why: That leaves the computer unprotected. Let it run and be patient.

wrong.text: Copy a quarantined file to your flash drive to show your friends.
wrong.why: That spreads the risk to other machines. Quarantined files stay where they are.

wrong.text: Install a cracked antivirus you found on a free download site.
wrong.why: Cracked programs are a common way to get infected. Use licensed or official software.

wrong.text: Open your friend's flash drive first, then scan it if something looks wrong.
wrong.why: Scan before you open anything. Files may run as soon as they are opened.

wrong.text: Click a pop-up saying that your computer is infected and pay to fix it.
wrong.why: Such pop-ups are often scams. Close the window and use the school's own antivirus.

distractors.name: Disk formatting utility
distractors.why: Formatting wipes a drive's data. That is not how you deal with a threat here.

distractors.name: Spreadsheet program
distractors.why: The scan is run in the antivirus program.

distractors.name: Screwdriver set
distractors.why: Nothing is opened in this job.

distractors.name: Windows installation disc
distractors.why: A scan does not need Windows to be reinstalled.

distractors.name: Free game downloaded from an unknown site
distractors.why: Unknown downloads are a common source of malware and have no place here.

decisions.prompt: The virus definitions will not update because the network is down. What do you do?

options.text: Report it, and hold off until the definitions can update
options.consequence: Definitions must be up to date first, or new threats can be missed.

options.text: Run the scan and write that the computer is clean
options.consequence: Old definitions miss new threats, so that result cannot be trusted.

options.text: Turn off the antivirus until the network returns
options.consequence: The computer now has no protection at all.

decisions.prompt: While the flash drive scan runs you spot a file on it named after your school. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for the scan to finish before opening anything
options.consequence: Nothing on the drive runs until the antivirus has checked it.

options.text: Open that file only, since it has a familiar name
options.consequence: A familiar name proves nothing. Opening files before a scan is a common mistake.

options.text: Stop the scan and copy the file onto the desktop
options.consequence: An unchecked file is now on the computer itself.

decisions.prompt: The Full scan is half-way through when the bell goes. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the teacher to let it run to the end
options.consequence: A full scan that is not interrupted checks every file.

options.text: Cancel it and record it as a completed scan
options.consequence: Half of the files were not checked, so your record is false.

options.text: Shut the computer down and restart it next week
options.consequence: The scan has been interrupted, and threats may still be there.

decisions.prompt: The program reports one threat and recommends quarantine. What do you do?

options.text: Quarantine it as the program advises
options.consequence: The file goes to a safe area where it cannot run.

options.text: Rename it so that it looks like a harmless file
options.consequence: A new name changes nothing. The threat is still there and still able to run.

options.text: Ignore it, as only one threat was found
options.consequence: One threat is enough to harm the computer and spread to others.

observations.prompt: Your report says a file has been quarantined. What does that mean?

options.text: It was moved to a safe area where it cannot run
It has been repaired and is safe to open now
options.why: Quarantine isolates a file. It does not make it safe.

options.text: It was copied to every drive for safe keeping
options.why: That would spread it. Quarantine isolates it.

options.text: It was sent out to other computers on the network
options.why: It is kept isolated on this computer.

observations.prompt: You confirm the firewall is on. What does this protect against?

options.text: Unauthorised traffic passing to or from the network
Infected files already on the hard disk
options.why: Finding those is the job of the antivirus. A firewall is not an antivirus.

options.text: Damage caused by a sudden power surge
options.why: That is the job of a UPS or surge protector.

numerics.prompt: {g} GB of data is scanned at {r} MB/s. How long does the scan take, in seconds? Use 1 GB = 1 024 MB.
{g} GB of data is scanned at {r} MB/s. How long does the scan take, in minutes? Use 1 GB = 1 024 MB.
A {g} GB flash drive is scanned at {r} MB/s. How many seconds does it take? Use 1 GB = 1 024 MB.

faults.scenario: Chika's computer picked up a virus after she brought in a borrowed flash drive. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She opened the files on the flash drive before scanning it.
lines.why: Scan first. Opening files on an unscanned drive is how infection spreads.

lines.text: She scanned without updating the virus definitions.
lines.why: Old definitions miss newer threats. Update first.

lines.text: She said that the firewall and the antivirus were the same thing.
lines.why: A firewall guards network traffic. Antivirus finds and removes malware.

lines.text: She checked that the firewall was on in Windows Security.
lines.why: That is the right place, and a sound check.

lines.text: She let the full scan run to the end.
lines.why: A full scan should not be interrupted.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions to take when scanning a computer for viruses.
written.explainPrompt: Why should the virus definitions be updated before scanning?
written.explainGuide: Definitions are the antivirus program's list of known threats. New malware appears all the time, so an out-of-date list can miss recent threats and wrongly report the computer as clean.
